Abstract. The rapid development of High-Performance Computing (HPC) has driven technological 
advancements but also brought environmental challenges such as high energy consumption, carbon 
emissions, and electronic waste. This paper develops three core models to systematically analyze 
these issues and proposes sustainable solutions. Firstly, the paper analyzes the total energy 
consumption of global HPC centers, dividing it into computing-related energy and non-computing 
energy (e.g., cooling systems). In 2024, the estimated total energy consumption of the HPC industry 
was 205 terawatt-hours, which could reach 287 to 328 terawatt-hours under full load conditions. 
Secondly, by calculating the carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour of electricity, the paper estimates 
the global carbon emissions of the HPC industry in 2024 to be 7.24 million tons. The third model 
assesses the environmental impact of electronic waste generated by HPC systems, projecting that 
by 2030, HPC-related electronic waste will produce 112.8 million tons of carbon emissions, with 
disposal costs reaching 715 million USD and landfill costs of 6 million USD. Additionally, the study 
predicts the trends of energy consumption, carbon emissions, and electronic waste in the HPC 
industry by 2030. The research indicates that by adopting energy-saving technologies, accelerating 
the transition to renewable energy, and optimizing electronic waste management, the HPC industry 
can mitigate environmental hazards while leveraging its innovative potential and, based on this, 
proposes technical design recommendations such as energy-efficient hardware and software, 
reducing electronic waste, adopting cloud storage, and considering environmental impacts in 
technical design. 
Keywords: HPC; carbon emissions; Economic benefits 
1. Introduction 
With the rapid development of artificial intelligence, data science, and cryptocurrency mining, 
High-Performance Computing (HPC) has become a core driver of global technological advancement. 
Still, this technical revolution has also presented unheard-of environmental problems. For example, 
the great energy demand has aggravated greenhouse gas emissions as well as several other problems 
including water use, electronic waste, rare resource extraction, and land use changes. Large volumes 
of water are used in data center cooling systems, and the manufacture and disposal of hardware cause 
the accumulation of difficultly recyclable electronic waste. Furthermore, the manufacturing of HPC 
gear depends on rare earth metal extraction, which not only harms the surroundings but also 
compromises ecosystems. More shockingly, environmental concerns could get more intense if the 
range of HPC applications keeps growing. 
This work presents a three-step framework based on Figure 1 to investigate High-Performance 
Computing (HPC) environmental impact. (1) Energy consumption analysis: It examines global HPC 
energy consumption, dividing it into computing-related energy and non-computing energy, primarily 
cooling systems. Under full-load settings, this study provides a baseline for knowledge of present 
consumption and future projections. (2) Carbon emission estimation: It calculates the emissions per 
kilowatt-hour (kWh) based on energy composition and carbon intensity, estimating carbon emissions. 
This stage emphasizes how urgently we should switch to renewable energy if we are to lower the

2. Literature Review 
High-powered computing systems are central in driving technological progress, but at a significant 
environmental cost. Quan et al. (2012) address the issue of high energy consumption and carbon 
emissions in data centers supporting traditional computing styles. Li et al. (2013) investigate the use 
of distributed generation techniques to provide clean energy to high-powered data centers, 
introducing data center power demand shaping as a novel technique to utilize onsite green energy 
efficiently. Uddin et al. (2012) introduced an Energy Efficiency and Low Carbon Enabler Green IT 
Framework for Data Centers Considering Green Metrics. Silva et al. (2024) continue to emphasize 
the critical need for decarbonizing HPC systems and improving their energy efficiency with strategies 
that include integrating renewable energy sources and waste heat reuse in large-scale HPC centers. 
Similarly, Oró et al. (2015) studied energy efficiency and renewable energy integration in data centers, 
focusing on strategies and modeling review. Goldman Sachs (2024) speculates the rapid advancement 
of AI technology is projected to drive a 160% increase in data center power demand by 2030, posing 
further challenges and emphasizing the urgency for sustainable energy solutions in HPC. 
3. Model I Energy consumption 
Energy consumption in an HPC center includes analyzing total power requirements, categorized 
into computing and non-computing energy. The computing energy encompasses the power used by 
compute nodes and storage systems involved in data processing, while non-computing energy covers 
the power needed for electronic waste and cooling infrastructure. So, this paper studies the total 
energy consumption of HPC from both computing and non-computing perspectives.

5.3 100% switch to renewable energy 
Then, based on our model, we continue to investigate the effects and potential challenges of a 100%

According to the model, switching to a 100% renewable energy source yields a 60% increase in

According to a report by Morgan Stanley. The global data center industry is projected to emit

In conclusion, based on the carbon intensity data for each energy source, transitioning from 
traditional energy mixes dominated by fossil fuels to a cleaner mix with 50% renewable energy could 
reduce the projected carbon emissions of the HPC industry by approximately 50% by 2030. Although 
this transition could significantly reduce carbon emissions, uncertainties remain in alleviating 
environmental pressure given the continued growth of demand, requiring further analysis of its 
comprehensive impact.

7. Conclusion and Policy Recommendations 
The rapid development of high-powered computing (HPC) has made it a cornerstone of 
technological advancement. Along with major environmental issues including high energy 
consumption, great carbon emissions, and the formation of electronic garbage (e-waste), this 
development is accompanied. Using three basic models, this work methodically explores these 
problems and suggests sustainable solutions. We first analyze the total energy consumption of HPC 
centers worldwide, separating computing-related energy from non-computing energy, which 
primarily involves cooling systems. Calculating electricity emissions per kilowatt-hour (kWh), both 
in the United States and worldwide, the second model approximates carbon emissions. Examining 
the relationship between data processing and hardware use helps the third model evaluate the 
environmental impact of e-waste produced by HPC systems. Focusing especially on 2030, the study 
uses these models to forecast future energy consumption, carbon emissions, and e-waste trends in the 
HPC sector, therefore helping one to grasp the long-term ecological consequences.  
Finally, based on the model findings, we propose actionable recommendations. Firstly, energy-
efficient hardware and software should be utilized to reduce the power consumption of HPC systems. 
Currently, over 40% of the energy consumption of HPC systems is used for cooling due to the 
significant heat they generate, leading to high energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions. 
Considerable energy savings can be achieved by using low-power processors, optimizing operating 
systems, and implementing efficient cooling systems. 
Secondly, regulate the disposal of HPC-related electronic waste. Electronic waste contains toxic 
substances such as lead and mercury, and landfilling releases harmful pollutants and generates many 
carbon emissions. Less than 16% of electronic waste is recycled annually, hence the need for 
sustainable practices such as recycling, refurbishing, and reusing equipment to reduce the generation 
of electronic waste. 
Thirdly, promote the transition to clean energy. The HPC industry relies on non-renewable energy 
sources like oil and coal, resulting in substantial carbon emissions. The U.S. Department of Energy 
has invested $3 million to promote industry collaboration with national laboratories to accelerate the 
development of clean energy technologies. More countries and regions are encouraged to follow suit 
and achieve a sustainable and carbon-neutral HPC industry.

Abstract: The rapid development of High-Performance Computing (HPC) has driven technological advancements but also brought environmental challenges such as high energy consumption, carbon emissions, and electronic waste. This paper develops three core models to systematically analyze these issues and proposes sustainable solutions. Firstly, the paper analyzes the total energy consumption of global HPC centers, dividing it into computing-related energy and non-computing energy (e.g., cooling systems). In 2024, the estimated total energy consumption of the HPC industry was 205 terawatt-hours, which could reach 287 to 328 terawatt-hours under full load conditions. Secondly, by calculating the carbon emissions per kilowatt-hour of electricity, the paper estimates the global carbon emissions of the HPC industry in 2024 to be 7.24 million tons. The third model assesses the environmental impact of electronic waste generated by HPC systems, projecting that by 2030, HPC-related electronic waste will produce 112.8 million tons of carbon emissions, with disposal costs reaching 715 million USD and landfill costs of 6 million USD. Additionally, the study predicts the trends of energy consumption, carbon emissions, and electronic waste in the HPC industry by 2030. The research indicates that by adopting energy-saving technologies, accelerating the transition to renewable energy, and optimizing electronic waste management, the HPC industry can mitigate environmental hazards while leveraging its innovative potential and, based on this, proposes technical design recommendations such as energy-efficient hardware and software, reducing electronic waste, adopting cloud storage, and considering environmental impacts in technical design.
